title: Social Engineering: hacking the human
description: Pretexting, vishing, MFA fatigue and the OSINT feeding it: why the weakest link is still a person.

1.title: Pretexting, vishing and influence principles
1.body:
## The script before the tool

A good social engineering attack is prepared like a pentest: recon
first. The OSINT from the previous room provides the material for the pretext:

- LinkedIn → org chart, who approves payments, who just joined
  (new hires say yes to everything).
- Corporate social media → trips, suppliers, projects ("I'm calling on behalf
  of the Delta project team you saw in the post").
- Website/public records → executives' ID/tax numbers, reception phone numbers,
  office hours.

With that, the **pretext** is built: a character, a context and a request
that fits both. "I'm David, from Microsoft 365 support, we've detected
an attempt to access your account and I need to verify a code"
works because every piece is plausible.

## Cialdini's principles applied to the attack

| Principle | In the attack |
|---|---|
| Authority | "I'm from the bank/IT/the police" |
| Urgency | "In 30 minutes everything gets locked" |
| Scarcity | "Only 2 spots left / it ends today" |
| Reciprocity | "I'll give you the report for free, just validate your email" |
| Social proof | "All your colleagues have already done it" |
| Commitment | "Can you confirm it's you? — great, now the code" |

Vishing = the call that combines authority + urgency against support or
finance. The famous real cases (Twitter 2020, Uber 2022) started
exactly like this: a convincing call to a helpdesk asking for an
MFA reset.

## Physical and in-person vectors

- **Tailgating**: slipping through the door right behind someone else's badge.
- **USB drops**: memory sticks planted in the parking lot ("nóminas_2026.xlsx -
  accelerator").
- **QR baiting** (quishing): codes that replace legitimate
  posters.

## The defender's side

The defenses that work are procedural, not technical: verification
channels (call BACK on the official number), limits on what is
NEVER requested by phone (nobody legitimate asks for MFA codes), blame-free
reporting, and measured simulations. The employee is not "the weakest link"
if the system is designed so that a single call is not enough.

social-engineering-t01-q01.prompt: What is the technique of building a credible identity/fake scenario before the contact?
social-engineering-t01-q01.hint: Pretexting — the script and the character that legitimize the request

social-engineering-t01-q02.prompt: What is social engineering over the phone called?
social-engineering-t01-q02.hint: Vishing (voice phishing) — smishing is the SMS version

social-engineering-t01-q03.prompt: Cialdini described 6 persuasion principles. Name the two exploited by 'I'm from the bank, there is ACTIVE fraud on your account right now' (answer in the form 'X and Y').
social-engineering-t01-q03.hint: Urgency/scarcity (act now) + authority (I'm your bank) — the others are reciprocity, commitment, liking and social proof

social-engineering-t01-q04.prompt: What is tailgating (or piggybacking) in physical security?
social-engineering-t01-q04.hint: Think about the courtesy of holding the door for whoever is behind you without asking for their badge.

options.a: Remotely cloning an employee's RFID card
options.b: Entering a controlled area by closely following someone authorized
options.c: Leaving infected USB sticks in the company's parking lot
options.d: Looking over someone's shoulder while they type their PIN

2.title: MFA fatigue, quishing and deepfakes
2.body:
## MFA is not the end: push fatigue

The MFA prompt has become the new battlefield. With valid
credentials (stuffing/phishing), the attacker fires approval prompts
in a loop:

```
23:47  Approve sign-in?  [Deny] [Accept]
23:48  Approve sign-in?  ...
23:52  ... (they sleep badly and accept "to make it stop")
```

Real cases (Uber 2022, Cisco 2022): purchased credentials +
a WhatsApp message to the target ("we're IT, you're about to get a prompt, accept it") +
push approved. Mitigations that work today:

- **Number matching** (the digit that has to match).
- A prompt with **context and location** ("are you in Moscow?").
- Rate limiting of prompts + an alert on bursts.

## Quishing: the QR that jumps the barriers

The QR code moves phishing out of email (where there is sandboxing, scanned URLs,
anti-spoofing) and onto the personal phone (where there is nothing). A poster in the
parking lot, a restaurant menu, a letter about a "new payroll portal" —
scanning is an almost reflexive act of trust. The URL behind it sometimes
isn't even looked at. Defense: URL extractors in the email gateway ALSO
for QR codes embedded in images + specific training.

## Deepfakes: forged authority

Voice synthesis (a 3-second sample is enough) and real-time video
have already been used for real fraud: the Arup scam ($25M in 2024) was
a full video call with deepfake "colleagues". Against this, the
procedure matters more than the technology:

- **Two-channel rule**: every financial instruction is confirmed
  through a second channel initiated by the recipient.
- Personal/per-team **code words** to verify each other on
  sensitive calls.
- Amount limits with asynchronous approval (not on the same call).

## The common framework

All these vectors share a structure: **forged authority +
urgency + a channel where verifying is hard**. Auditing processes with
that template (who can request what? how is it verified? what happens if
the channel is compromised?) is threat modeling applied to humans — the
perfect bridge to the threat modeling room.

social-engineering-t02-q01.prompt: What does the MFA fatigue (push bombing) attack consist of?
social-engineering-t02-q01.hint: Picture the victim receiving one approval notification after another at 3am.

options.a: Cloning the victim's SIM to receive their SMS codes
options.c: Sending bursts of MFA prompts until the victim approves one to make them stop
options.d: Stealing the victim's phone to approve the login

social-engineering-t02-q02.prompt: Which MFA app setting eliminates push bombing by requiring a number shown on screen to be matched?
social-engineering-t02-q02.hint: Number matching (shows a number you must type on your phone) — Microsoft enabled it by default in 2023

social-engineering-t02-q03.prompt: What is phishing via QR codes called?
social-engineering-t02-q03.hint: Quishing (QR + phishing): it bypasses email link scanners and lands on the personal phone, outside MDM

social-engineering-t02-q04.prompt: What makes voice/video deepfakes especially effective against financial approval processes?
social-engineering-t02-q04.hint: Remember the Arup case in 2024 ($25M): a full video call with fake 'colleagues'.

options.a: They impersonate authority (CEO/CFO) in real time and defeat call-back verification
options.b: They carry embedded malware that approves the payment automatically
options.c: They only work if the victim has no antivirus
options.d: They are always sent from the company's legitimate email domain
